title: Communicating Equity Findings with Care and Public Trust
before: Explore how DSD staff communicate equity findings accurately, keeping the comparison, base, uncertainty, and people’s accounts visible.

turns.text: This discussion opens Communicating Equity Findings with Care and Public Trust. It’s about explaining research, policy, service, or workforce findings so readers understand what the evidence shows and what it doesn’t. The course starts with a small phrase. A report records fewer completed requests from one route, and the draft says, “Those users do not follow through.”

And that phrase does a lot of work. The records describe an event, not why it happened, yet the sentence points readers toward the people and away from the route. So the course asks what condition a sentence invites readers to examine, and what condition it hides. That question carries through the rest of the slides.

A key distinction is between observation, interpretation, and cause. An observation states what was found in a defined source. An interpretation explains what it may mean. A causal claim says what produced it. Readers should be able to tell these apart. A possible systemic mechanism can guide inquiry without becoming an established finding.

The course uses invented figures to make that concrete. Two practice routes have the same number of recorded clarification offers, but very different numbers of requests. So equal counts can sit on different bases. You’ll work with those figures, decide what a recorded offer establishes, and see what a combined overall percentage can hide about the separate routes.

Missing information gets its own attention. If no account of understanding is supplied, that information is unknown, not zero and not favorable. The course warns against letting a polished chart make a record seem more complete than it is. It also asks us to state what was counted, the base, the period, and the source, using the same scope whenever we compare.

Then there’s a rewrite of a deficit explanation. You’ll replace a line like “people failed to follow our instructions” with the actual instruction, the difficulty observed, and the person’s account where it exists. The course is careful to say that softening the label isn’t enough. “Engagement challenges” can carry the same unsupported explanation in quieter words.

Workforce findings come up too. A practice draft calls a retention difference a problem with employees’ commitment, without job mix, period comparisons, or employee accounts. You’ll consider what a stronger account would look like. The course points out that a retention difference might involve different jobs, periods, opportunities, or reporting coverage, and doesn’t identify a cause by itself.

Stories need the same care. A personal account can explain the meaning of an experience, but it doesn’t establish how often everyone experiences it. The course cautions against stories that cast the organization as rescuing someone from a problem located only in them. You’ll practice with a draft story that turns a participant’s request for a clearer route into something else.

Accessibility and privacy are part of a faithful account. A chart needs an understandable account of its essential values and limits, and color shouldn’t carry the message alone. Before sharing a record or story, we use the applicable review and permissions. Names aren’t the only details that identify someone, and an appealing narrative doesn’t authorize publication.

Near the end, you’ll draft two sentences in your own words: what the evidence shows, and what the reader should examine next, including the base and one meaningful limit. Then you’ll check whether you slipped in a cause, a motive, an endorsement, or a promised result. Keeping findings current matters too, so an old claim doesn’t quietly describe the present.

As you go, think of a finding you’ve shared or read recently, maybe in a report, a briefing, or a team update. What was compared, and what was the base? Bring that example along. The aim is communication that leads with what matters, keeps people’s dignity and accounts intact, and is honest about what remains unknown.

guidance.title: Keeping three kinds of claims apart
guidance.text: When you review a draft, try marking each sentence as an observation, an interpretation, or a cause. Observations should name a source. Interpretations should read as possibilities. Causal claims need evidence that actually supports them. If a sentence moves from what was recorded to why it happened without that evidence, rewrite it as a question the next inquiry can examine.

guidance.title: What would a reader take away?
guidance.text: Think of a finding you might explain to leadership, a partner, or the public. When a reader finishes your account, what would they believe happened, and why? Would they also see what remains unknown and what happens next? Consider whether your wording acknowledges progress and unresolved conditions together, without declaring trust or improved equity on the report’s behalf.
